title: 22. Interview: gRPC
summary: Interview Q&A for gRPC — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 gRPC interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is gRPC, and how does it differ from REST?
**Answer:** gRPC is Google's RPC framework that uses HTTP/2 as the transport and Protocol Buffers as the wire format. You write a `.proto` file declaring the service interface and message types; `protoc` generates client stubs and server interfaces in your language. The client calls the stub like a local function — `user = stub.GetUser(req)` — and gRPC handles serialization, transport, and deserialization. Differences from REST: (1) **Wire format** — gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (binary, ~3-10x smaller than JSON, schema-required); REST typically uses JSON (text, human-readable, schema-optional). (2) **Transport** — gRPC uses HTTP/2 with multiplexed streams (many concurrent RPCs on one TCP connection); REST typically uses HTTP/1.1 (one request per connection, head-of-line blocking). (3) **Contract** — gRPC's `.proto` is the source of truth, code is generated; REST's contract is informal (OpenAPI specs bolted on after). (4) **Streaming** — gRPC supports unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidi-streaming; REST is unary only (request-response). (5) **Browser support** — gRPC cannot be called directly from browsers (requires gRPC-Web proxy); REST works in any browser. (6) **Performance** — gRPC is typically 2-10x lower latency and bandwidth than REST/JSON. Use gRPC for internal service-to-service (Netflix, etcd, Kubernetes); REST for public APIs (browser, mobile, third-party devs).
**Visual:**
```
gRPC:                          REST:
.proto (schema) -> codegen     OpenAPI (bolted on after)
HTTP/2 multiplexed streams     HTTP/1.1 (one req per conn)
Protobuf binary (~10 bytes)    JSON text (~80 bytes for same data)
unary + 3 streaming types      unary only
not browser-callable           browser-callable
2-10x faster                    simple, ubiquitous
```

### Q2. What are Protocol Buffers, and how do they compare to JSON?
**Answer:** Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) is Google's language-agnostic binary serialization format. You define message types in a `.proto` file (`message User { int64 id = 1; string name = 2; }`); the compiler generates code in your language; you serialize with `user.SerializeToString()` and deserialize with `User.FromString(bytes)`. Comparison with JSON: (1) **Size** — Protobuf is typically 3-10x smaller than JSON for the same data because it uses binary encoding (varint for integers, length-prefixed strings) and does not repeat field names (fields are identified by number, not name). A `User{id:42, name:"Ada", email:"ada@example.com"}` is ~25 bytes in Protobuf vs ~65 bytes in JSON. (2) **Speed** — Protobuf serialization is 2-5x faster than JSON parsing because it is a simple binary copy, not a text parse. (3) **Schema** — Protobuf requires a schema (the `.proto` file); JSON does not (but JSON Schema can be bolted on). The schema is the contract, enabling code generation, type safety, and cross-language interop. (4) **Human-readable** — JSON is; Protobuf is not (you need to deserialize to inspect). (5) **Schema evolution** — both support additive changes (new fields are safe); Protobuf has explicit rules (reserve field numbers when removing fields, never reuse numbers, use `optional` for new fields). (6) **Ecosystem** — JSON has universal tooling (every language, every database); Protobuf is well-supported but less universal. Use Protobuf for internal RPC (gRPC), and JSON for public APIs where human-readability and tooling matter.
**Visual:**
```
User {id: 42, name: "Ada", email: "ada@example.com"}

Protobuf (binary, 25 bytes):
  08 2A 12 03 41 64 61 1A 10 61 64 61 40 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 2E 63 6F 6D
  (field 1 = 42, field 2 = "Ada", field 3 = "ada@example.com")

JSON (text, 65 bytes):
  {"id":42,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com"}
  (field names repeated in every payload)

Protobuf: smaller, faster, schema-required, binary, not human-readable
JSON:     larger, slower, schema-optional, text, human-readable
```

### Q3. What are the four RPC types in gRPC, and when do you use each?
**Answer:** (1) **Unary** — single request, single response. `rpc GetUser(GetUserRequest) returns (User)`. This is the typical RPC, analogous to a function call or a REST GET. Use for: read a single record, perform a computation, submit a transaction. The vast majority of gRPC calls are unary. (2) **Server streaming** — single request, stream of responses. `rpc ListOrders(ListOrdersRequest) returns (stream Order)`. The server sends a sequence of messages; the client reads them as an iterator. Use for: paginated result sets (avoid loading 100k records into memory), live updates (stock prices, log streams), large file downloads. etcd's Watch API is server-streaming — clients subscribe to key changes and receive a stream of events. (3) **Client streaming** — stream of requests, single response. `rpc UploadChunks(stream Chunk) returns (UploadSummary)`. The client sends a sequence of messages; the server aggregates and responds once. Use for: file upload (stream chunks instead of buffering the whole file), batched writes (send 1000 records, server commits once), telemetry ingestion. (4) **Bidirectional streaming** — both sides stream. `rpc Chat(stream Message) returns (stream Message)`. Use for: chat apps, multiplayer games, real-time collaboration, any case where either side may send at any time. All four run over HTTP/2 streams, so they are all multiplexed on a single TCP connection — you can have 100 concurrent unary calls OR a chat stream + 50 unary calls, all on the same connection.
**Visual:**
```
Unary:           client ---req---> server
                 client <---resp--- server

Server streaming:  client ---req---> server
                   client <---msg1--- server
                   client <---msg2--- server
                   client <---msg3--- server  (etcd Watch)

Client streaming:  client ---msg1---> server
                   client ---msg2---> server
                   client ---msg3---> server
                   client <---resp--- server   (file upload)

Bidi streaming:    client <---> server         (chat)
                   both sides send messages interleaved
```

### Q4. What are gRPC interceptors, and how do you use them?
**Answer:** Interceptors are gRPC's middleware — code that runs before (or after) every RPC, without modifying the application logic. They are the equivalent of Express middleware, Django middleware, or Spring AOP. There are two kinds on the server side: **unary interceptors** (run on unary calls) and **stream interceptors** (run on streaming calls). On the client side, similarly. Use cases: (1) **Logging and observability** — every RPC is logged with method name, latency, status code, and trace ID; emit Prometheus metrics (request count, latency histogram, error rate). (2) **Authentication** — extract a JWT or mTLS client identity from the request metadata, validate it, and attach the caller's identity to the request context. (3) **Rate limiting** — apply per-caller token buckets before the handler runs. (4) **Tracing** — propagate OpenTelemetry trace context across services (extract trace ID from `grpc-trace-bin` header, attach span, inject on downstream calls). (5) **Retry** — wrap unary calls in a retry policy (e.g., retry on `UNAVAILABLE` up to 3 times with exponential backoff). (6) **Circuit breaking** — trip a circuit breaker when a backend's error rate exceeds a threshold. (7) **Validation** — validate request fields before the handler runs. Netflix's internal gRPC framework (armeria) wraps every call with decorators for tracing, retries, circuit breakers, and request-level timeouts. Envoy's gRPC filter is essentially a network-level interceptor that does the same. Interceptors compose: you can stack logging + auth + tracing + rate-limit + retry, each as a separate interceptor.
**Visual:**
```
client -> [auth interceptor] -> [log interceptor] -> [trace interceptor]
        -> [rate-limit interceptor] -> [handler]
        <- response propagates back through same chain

Each interceptor: def intercept(self, req, handler):
    # pre-processing (extract JWT, start span, check rate limit)
    resp = handler(req)
    # post-processing (log, record span, emit metric)
    return resp
```

### Q5. What are deadlines in gRPC, and why are they mandatory?
**Answer:** A deadline is the absolute time by which an RPC must complete (e.g., "complete by 12:00:01.500 UTC"). The client sets it with `context.with_timeout(context, timedelta(seconds=1))` or `context.with_deadline(time.time() + 1)`. gRPC propagates the deadline downstream: if service A calls service B with a 1-second deadline, and B calls C 200 ms in, B's call to C inherits a deadline of 800 ms (the remaining time). When a deadline expires, gRPC cancels the call — the client receives `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, the server's handler receives a cancellation signal and should abort its work, and any downstream calls are also cancelled. Deadlines are mandatory because without them, a slow downstream service cascades failures: client calls A, A calls B, B is slow; the client retries A, A calls B again, B is still slow; soon the client has 100 outstanding calls to A, A has 100 to B, B is overwhelmed and dies. With deadlines, the client gives up after 1 second, A gives up after 800 ms, B gives up after 600 ms — the slow service recovers because callers back off. The #1 production gotcha with gRPC is forgetting to set deadlines — by default gRPC has no deadline, so a hung downstream service hangs the caller forever. Best practice: every RPC must have a deadline, set explicitly by the client, tuned per call (1s for fast reads, 30s for slow writes). Combined with retries (with their own deadlines) and circuit breakers, this is the foundation of distributed reliability.
**Visual:**
```
client (deadline: 1.0s)
   |--- calls A at t=0
   A (deadline inherited: 1.0s)
      |--- calls B at t=200ms
      B (deadline inherited: 0.8s)
         |--- calls C at t=350ms
         C (deadline inherited: 0.65s)
            |--- C is slow, takes 800ms
            at t=1.0s: client deadline expires
            -> client receives DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
            -> A's call to B cancelled
            -> B's call to C cancelled
            -> C aborts its work (no wasted CPU)
```

### Q6. How does gRPC load balancing work, and why is it different from REST?
**Answer:** gRPC uses persistent HTTP/2 connections — a client opens one TCP connection to a backend and reuses it for many concurrent RPCs (multiplexed streams). This is efficient (no TCP slow-start per RPC) but breaks L4 load balancing: if a client opens one connection to a backend pool fronted by an L4 LB (e.g., AWS NLB), the LB routes the connection to ONE backend, and ALL subsequent RPCs from that client go to the same backend — defeating load distribution. Three solutions. (1) **Client-side load balancing** — the client knows about ALL backends (via DNS, xDS, or a name resolver) and picks one per RPC. gRPC's built-in `round_robin` policy does this. Works well for internal meshes where clients are gRPC-aware. (2) **L7 proxy** — Envoy, gRPC-native LBs (Envoy, Linkerd, Traefik) understand HTTP/2 and route per-stream (per-RPC), not per-connection. The client opens one connection to the proxy; the proxy opens connections to many backends and routes each RPC to a different backend. This is the standard in service meshes. (3) **Proxyless** — newer gRPC supports xDS (Envoy's API) directly in the client, so the client gets backend list and load info from a control plane (Istio, Traffic Director) without a proxy. This is the future but requires xDS-aware clients. For REST/HTTP-1.1, L4 LBs work fine because each request opens a new connection. The gotcha: if you front a gRPC service with an L4 LB (NLB) without proxy or client-side LB, you will get uneven load distribution — some backends get all the traffic, others sit idle. Always use an L7 proxy or client-side LB for gRPC.
**Visual:**
```
L4 LB (broken for gRPC):
   client --1 TCP conn--> [L4 LB] --> backend A   (ALL RPCs go to A)
                                       backend B   (idle)
                                       backend C   (idle)
   (LB routes per-connection, not per-RPC)

L7 proxy (correct):
   client --1 conn--> [Envoy] --per-RPC--> backend A
                              --per-RPC--> backend B
                              --per-RPC--> backend C
   (Envoy understands HTTP/2, routes per-stream)

Client-side LB (also correct):
   client knows [A, B, C] --per-RPC round-robin--> A, B, C, A, B, C, ...
```

### Q7. How do you evolve a gRPC service without breaking clients?
**Answer:** Protocol Buffers has explicit compatibility rules. **Safe changes**: (1) Add a new field — old clients ignore it, new clients populate it; (2) Add a new RPC method — old clients don't call it; (3) Remove a field — `reserve` its number and name so it's never reused (`reserved 3; reserved "old_field_name";`); (4) Change a field from `optional` to `required` (in proto3, all fields are optional by default); (5) Rename a field (the wire format uses field numbers, not names). **Breaking changes** (require a new major version): (1) Change a field's type (e.g., `int32` to `string`); (2) Change a field's number (the wire format keys on number); (3) Remove a field without reserving its number (a future field could reuse it and confuse old clients); (4) Change an RPC's signature (request/response type); (5) Make a previously-optional field required. **Best practices**: (1) Never reuse field numbers — when you remove a field, `reserve` its number forever; (2) Use `optional` for new fields so old clients don't send default values that the server might interpret as "set to zero"; (3) Use `oneof` for mutually exclusive fields; (4) Version your `.proto` package (`package usersvc.v1;` -> `package usersvc.v2;`) when you make breaking changes, and run both versions side-by-side while clients migrate; (5) Use Buf's breaking-change detector in CI to catch regressions. Google's internal rule: every proto change must pass a compatibility check, and breaking changes require a new package version with a 12-month migration window.
**Visual:**
```
Safe (non-breaking):
   + new field        -> old clients ignore, new clients populate
   + new RPC method   -> old clients don't call
   - removed field    -> reserve its number: "reserved 3;"
   rename field       -> wire format keys on number, not name

Breaking (require v2):
   change field type  -> int32 -> string (wire format mismatch)
   change field number-> field 3 -> field 4 (old clients send wrong field)
   remove without reserve -> future field reuses number -> data corruption
   change RPC signature -> different request/response type

Best practice: package usersvc.v1; -> package usersvc.v2; for breaking
               run both side-by-side, 12-month migration window
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your e-commerce site has 50 microservices. The checkout flow makes 7 sequential REST/JSON calls taking 800 ms total. The team wants to cut this to 200 ms. How would gRPC help?
**Answer:** Two main wins. (1) **Per-call latency reduction** — gRPC's Protobuf serialization is 2-5x faster than JSON parsing, and HTTP/2 multiplexing avoids TCP slow-start on every call (a REST call over a fresh TCP connection spends 50-100 ms in slow-start; a gRPC call on a warm HTTP/2 connection is sub-millisecond on the transport layer). A REST call that takes 100 ms typically drops to 30-50 ms in gRPC. (2) **Parallelization** — HTTP/2 multiplexing lets the client issue all 7 calls concurrently on one TCP connection, then wait for all responses (using `concurrent.futures` or async). If the calls are independent (fetch user, fetch cart, fetch inventory, fetch shipping options), they all run in parallel; the total latency is the slowest call, not the sum. Sequential REST: 7 × 100 ms = 700 ms; parallel gRPC: max(call times) ≈ 50 ms. Trade-offs: (1) The 7 services must expose gRPC APIs — significant migration work if they are REST-only. (2) The 7 calls must actually be independent — if call 4 depends on call 3's result, you cannot parallelize. (3) Error handling is harder — if one of 7 parallel calls fails, you must decide whether to fail the whole checkout or degrade gracefully. Netflix's checkout migration from REST to gRPC in 2018 reported exactly this pattern — 2-3x lower latency and 60-70% lower bandwidth. For the calls that cannot be parallelized (sequential dependencies), consider collapsing them into a single gRPC call that the server handles internally — one network hop instead of seven.
**Visual:**
```
REST/JSON (sequential, 700ms):
   client -> [100ms] -> A -> [100ms] -> B -> [100ms] -> C -> ... -> G
   total: 7 x 100ms = 700ms (TCP slow-start per call)

gRPC (parallel, ~50ms):
   client --(HTTP/2 multiplexed)--> A (50ms)
                                --> B (40ms)
                                --> C (50ms)   ... all in parallel
                                --> G (30ms)
   total: max(call times) = 50ms   (one TCP conn, no slow-start)
```

### Q2. You are building a chat application where users send messages and receive messages from others in real time. Why is gRPC bidi streaming a good fit?
**Answer:** Bidi streaming (`rpc Chat(stream Message) returns (stream Message)`) lets both client and server send messages at any time over a single long-lived HTTP/2 stream. The client opens the stream, sends a message, and the server can push back a message immediately — no polling, no extra round-trips, no HTTP/1.1 connection-per-message overhead. Compare alternatives: (1) REST with polling — client polls `GET /messages?since=<ts>` every 1 second; latency is up to 1 second, bandwidth is wasted on empty polls. (2) REST with long-polling — client holds a `GET /messages` open until a message arrives; works but is fragile (each message requires a new HTTP request). (3) WebSockets — works in browsers but is a separate protocol from your REST/gRPC API; you end up maintaining two stacks. (4) Server-Sent Events (SSE) — server-to-client only; the client still needs a separate channel for sending messages. gRPC bidi streaming handles both directions in one stream, with the same Protobuf schema, same auth, same tracing, same interceptors as your other RPCs. Discord uses gRPC bidi streaming for its chat backbone; Slack uses a similar pattern. Trade-offs: (1) the stream is stateful — the load balancer must keep the same client on the same server (sticky); if the server dies, the client must reconnect and re-establish state. (2) Browser support requires gRPC-Web with streaming, which is more complex than unary gRPC-Web. (3) Backpressure — if a client is slow to consume, the server must buffer or drop; gRPC has built-in flow control but you must handle it. (4) Authorization must be re-checked on every message, not just at stream open.
**Visual:**
```
gRPC bidi streaming chat:
   client <=======stream=======> server
   client: send("hello")        -> server broadcasts to room
   server: push("hi from Bob")  -> client renders
   server: push("Alice joined") -> client renders
   (one long-lived HTTP/2 stream, both directions, no polling)

vs REST polling:
   client: GET /messages  -> []  (empty)
   client: GET /messages  -> []  (empty)
   client: GET /messages  -> [{msg: "hello"}]
   (1s latency, wasted bandwidth on empty polls)
```

### Q3. You have a Kafka-like log ingestion service that receives 100,000 events per second from 1000 clients. Should you use gRPC client streaming or REST?
**Answer:** gRPC client streaming is the better fit. Each client opens a stream and sends events as a continuous sequence of Protobuf messages; the server batches them and commits to the log periodically. Benefits: (1) **Bandwidth** — Protobuf is 3-10x smaller than JSON, so 100k events/sec at 200 bytes/event (Protobuf) is 20 MB/s vs 100 MB/s for JSON. At 1000 clients, this saves significant network capacity. (2) **Connection efficiency** — one HTTP/2 connection per client carries the entire stream; REST would require either one connection per event (catastrophic) or batching with HTTP/1.1 keep-alive (still one TCP connection per client, but no streaming semantics). (3) **Server-side batching** — the server's stream handler receives messages as they arrive and can batch-commit to the log every 100ms or 1000 messages, whichever comes first. With REST, each event is a separate request, so batching requires client-side buffering. (4) **Backpressure** — HTTP/2 flow control lets the server signal "slow down" if it cannot keep up; the client respects it automatically. Trade-offs: (1) if a client's stream breaks mid-batch, you need to handle resend logic (dedupe by event ID); (2) the server must handle slow consumers without OOM — set a buffer cap and drop or backpressure; (3) for browser-based clients, gRPC-Web does not support client streaming well — use a custom WebSocket or REST-with-batching for browsers. Kafka itself uses a custom binary protocol over TCP (not gRPC), but the design rationale is identical — binary framing, streaming, backpressure. Stripe's event ingestion uses gRPC client streaming from internal services.
**Visual:**
```
1000 clients, each streaming 100 events/sec:
   client 1 ---stream of Protobuf events---> [ingest server] --batch commit--> log
   client 2 ---stream of Protobuf events--->                  (every 1000 msgs)
   ...
   client 1000 ---stream of Protobuf events--->

benefits: 1 conn per client, 3-10x smaller than JSON, server-side batching,
          HTTP/2 flow control for backpressure.
```

### Q4. Your team serves a gRPC API to external customers. Some customers report intermittent `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` errors. How do you debug?
**Answer:** Three layers to check. (1) **Client-side deadline too aggressive** — the customer's client may be setting a 100ms deadline when the call legitimately takes 200ms (e.g., a database read that hits a slow disk). Ask the customer what deadline they set; if it's too low, have them bump it to 1s for read calls. (2) **Server-side latency** — instrument the server's handler with histograms (Prometheus `grpc_server_handling_seconds_bucket`) and look at p99 latency. If p99 is 500ms and the customer's deadline is 200ms, you have a real performance problem: a slow DB query, a downstream service call without its own deadline, or GC pressure. Fix by adding indexes, parallelizing downstream calls, or tuning the JVM/Go runtime. (3) **Network** — between client and server, intermediate proxies (Envoy, ALB) may have their own timeouts that are shorter than the gRPC deadline; check the proxy config. If the proxy times out at 100ms, the customer sees `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` even though the gRPC server is still working. Specific debug steps: (a) add structured logging on both sides with a request ID and timing breakdown (auth 5ms, handler 180ms, downstream 150ms); (b) use OpenTelemetry tracing to see exactly where time is spent across the call chain; (c) check gRPC's built-in metrics (`grpc_server_handled_total{grpc_code="DEADLINE_EXCEEDED"}`) to see the error rate by method; (d) test from the customer's network if possible — a flaky intermediate network (packet loss, congested peering) can cause timeouts. The most common root cause in practice is "the customer set a deadline but the server has no deadline on its downstream calls, so a slow DB query hangs the whole chain."
**Visual:**
```
Customer deadline: 200ms
Server p99 latency: 500ms
-> DEADLINE_EXCEEDED for ~10% of calls

Debug chain:
   client (200ms deadline)
     -> server handler (start)
        -> db query (no deadline, takes 450ms)  <-- here
     -> server handler returns at 450ms
   client already gave up at 200ms

Fix: set deadline on db query (300ms), add index, parallelize downstream calls
```

### Q5. You are running a gRPC service behind an AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB). Some backends are overloaded while others are idle. Why?
**Answer:** This is the classic gRPC load-balancing gotcha. NLB is an L4 load balancer — it routes per TCP connection, not per request. gRPC clients open ONE persistent HTTP/2 connection to the NLB and reuse it for all RPCs (multiplexed streams). The NLB routes that connection to ONE backend, and ALL subsequent RPCs from that client go to that same backend. If you have 100 clients each opening one connection, and 10 backends, you get an uneven distribution — some backends get 20 connections, others get 5, depending on the NLB's hashing. The fix: use an L7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 and routes per-stream (per-RPC). Options: (1) **Envoy** — sits in front of the backends, terminates the client's HTTP/2 connection, and opens its own connections to all backends, routing each RPC to a different backend. This is what Istio, Linkerd, and Consul Connect do under the hood. (2) **AWS ALB** — supports HTTP/2 and gRPC natively (since 2020), routes per-request. Replace the NLB with an ALB. (3) **Client-side load balancing** — the client's gRPC channel uses `grpc.lb_policy_name=round_robin` and the name resolver returns all backend IPs; the client picks a different backend per RPC. This works but requires the client to be gRPC-aware and to know all backends (via DNS that returns all IPs, or xDS). Netflix uses client-side LB with their Eureka service discovery; Google uses xDS. The simplest fix in AWS: switch from NLB to ALB. Trade-off: ALB adds ~1ms latency vs NLB's ~0.5ms, and ALB has a per-request cost. The extra 0.5ms is worth it for correct load distribution.
**Visual:**
```
NLB (L4, broken for gRPC):
   client 1 --1 TCP conn--> [NLB] --> backend A   (all RPCs to A)
   client 2 --1 TCP conn--> [NLB] --> backend A   (NLB hashed to A again)
   client 3 --1 TCP conn--> [NLB] --> backend C
   backend A: 2 clients' worth of traffic (overloaded)
   backend B: 0 clients (idle)

ALB or Envoy (L7, correct):
   client 1 --1 conn--> [ALB] --per-RPC--> A, B, C, A, B, C, ...
   client 2 --1 conn--> [ALB] --per-RPC--> B, C, A, B, C, A, ...
   (each RPC routed independently; even distribution)
```

### Q6. You want to expose a gRPC service to browser-based JavaScript clients. How?
**Answer:** Browsers do not expose HTTP/2 trailers (which gRPC uses for status codes), so gRPC cannot be called directly from JavaScript. Use **gRPC-Web**, a protocol variant that translates between browser-friendly HTTP/1.1 (or HTTP/2 without trailers) and real gRPC. Architecture: browser JS calls a gRPC-Web client (generated by `protoc-gen-grpc-web`); the call goes to an Envoy proxy (or a special gRPC-Web proxy) as an HTTP POST; the proxy translates it to a real gRPC call to the backend; the response is translated back to gRPC-Web format and returned to the browser. Limitations: (1) **Streaming support is limited** — gRPC-Web originally supported only unary and server streaming; client streaming and bidi streaming require a WebSocket fallback or the new gRPC-Web streaming spec. For real-time apps, WebSockets may be simpler. (2) **Proxy required** — you must run Envoy (or the gRPC-Web proxy) in front of the backend. Envoy has a `grpc_web` filter that does the translation. (3) **CORS** — if the proxy is on a different origin than the browser app, you must configure CORS on the proxy. (4) **Binary response** — gRPC-Web responses are binary (Protobuf); the browser must support `Content-Type: application/grpc-web+proto`. Trade-offs: if your browser client is the only consumer, REST or GraphQL is simpler (no proxy, native browser support). If you have a gRPC service that you want to reuse for both internal (gRPC) and browser (gRPC-Web) clients, gRPC-Web is the right choice — same `.proto`, same server, just a proxy in front. Google Cloud Endpoints and gRPC-Gateway are alternatives that generate a REST facade from the `.proto`.
**Visual:**
```
Browser JS  --gRPC-Web (HTTP POST, no trailers)-->  [Envoy proxy]
                                                       | (translate)
                                                       v
                                                    [gRPC server]
                                                       | (real gRPC)
                                                       v
                                                    [backend]

Alternatives:
   gRPC-Gateway: generates REST endpoints from .proto (REST facade)
   Connect (Buf): newer protocol that works without proxy in browser
```

### Q7. You are designing the inter-node communication protocol for a new distributed database (like CockroachDB or TiKV). Why would you choose gRPC over a custom binary protocol?
**Answer:** CockroachDB and TiKV both use gRPC for inter-node communication, and the rationale is instructive. (1) **Streaming for replication** — Raft consensus requires the leader to stream log entries to followers; gRPC server streaming is a perfect fit (`rpc RaftStep(stream RaftMessage) returns (stream RaftMessage)`). A custom protocol would need to design its own streaming framing. (2) **Bidirectional for gossip** — cluster membership and metadata gossip is naturally bidi-streaming (`rpc Gossip(stream GossipMessage) returns (stream GossipMessage)`). (3) **Schema as documentation** — the `.proto` file documents every message type and RPC, making the codebase readable for new contributors. (4) **Cross-language** — TiKV is Rust, but its clients are Go, Java, Python, Rust; gRPC's code generation gives all of them type-safe stubs. (5) **Built-in features** — deadlines, cancellation, interceptors, tracing, metrics, health checking all come for free; a custom protocol must build them. (6) **HTTP/2 multiplexing** — a node can have 1000 outstanding RPCs to another node on a single TCP connection, which is critical for high-throughput replication. Trade-offs: (1) Protobuf is not the most efficient for very small messages (the framing overhead is ~5-10 bytes per message, which matters at millions of messages per second); some databases use custom protocols with tighter encoding for hot paths. (2) gRPC's threading model may not match the database's async runtime perfectly — TiKV uses tokio with gRPC's async API, which works but requires care. (3) The dependency tree of grpcio is heavy (bundles boringssl, etc.). For most databases, gRPC's benefits outweigh the costs — CockroachDB, TiKV, etcd, FoundationDB (custom but similar), and YugaByte all use gRPC or a similar RPC framework.
**Visual:**
```
Distributed DB nodes (gRPC inter-node):
   node1 <--RaftStep (server stream)--> node2  (log replication)
   node1 <--Gossip (bidi stream)-------> node3  (membership gossip)
   node1 <--QueryPlan (unary)---------> node4  (cross-shard query)
   node1 <--LeaseKeepAlive (unary)----> node5  (every 5s)

All on persistent HTTP/2 connections, multiplexed.
Built-in: deadlines, cancellation, tracing, health checks, interceptors.
Used by: CockroachDB, TiKV, etcd, YugaByte.
```

quiz.explanation: gRPC is Google's RPC framework that uses HTTP/2 as the transport and Protocol Buffers as the wire format. You write a .proto file declaring the service interface and message types; protoc generates client stubs and server interfaces in your language. The client calls the stub like a local function — user = stub.GetUser(req) — and gRPC handles serialization, transport, and deserialization.

They are the equivalent of Express middleware, Django middleware, or Spring AOP. There are two kinds on the server side: unary interceptors (run on unary calls) and stream interceptors (run on streaming calls).

quiz.explanation: A deadline is the absolute time by which an RPC must complete (e.g., "complete by 12:00:01.500 UTC"). The client sets it with context.with_timeout(context, timedelta(seconds=1)) or context.with_deadline(time.time() + 1). gRPC propagates the deadline downstream: if service A calls service B with a 1-second deadline, and B calls C 200 ms in, B's call to C inherits a deadline of 800 ms (the remaining time).
